thread.title: UPDATE: Here's a thought: Maybe the stock market won't crash this year because it can't

author: morningstar.com
title: UPDATE: Here's a thought: Maybe the stock market won't crash this year because it can't
text:
By Shawn Langlois, MarketWatch
Critical information for the U.S. trading day
Just when it feels like the market might finally topple and give desperate bears their long-awaited told-ya-so moment, a stubborn streak like the one the Dow is currently riding proves again who has the upper hand: The bulls.
Yes, despite all the hand-wringing over tightening, lofty valuations, nasty politics, [insert any number of reasons to sell], this market still belongs to the bulls. The blue chips' stretch of seven positive sessions (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/dows-bid-for-7th-straight-winning-session-in-play-2018-05-11)is the longest run since November of last year, and much of the backbone of this little rally can be attributed to a steady diet of stellar corporate earnings.
Whether it can continue is another question, but there's a strong case to be made this market has a backstop in the explosion of buybacks lately.
It's still early, but, according to Goldman Sachs (GS), S&P 500 companies are on track to announce a record $650 billion in buybacks this year. Apple (AAPL), just to name one, is already out there with its massive $100 billion program.
Here's a graphic from a Barron's piece on the subject (https://www.barrons.com/articles/why-the-buyback-boom-is-bullish-for-investors-1526089472):
"With this kind of corporate buying pressure in the market, it's very hard for shares to crash," writes Wolf Richter of the Wolf Street blog (https://wolfstreet.com/2018/05/13/why-i-think-the-stock-market-cannot-crash-in-2018/) in our call of the day. "Companies will pile into the market at every dip and buy as high as possible. It's unlikely the overall market can crash this year no matter what happens."
Historically, companies that buy back their own shares outperform the broader market. The Wall Street Journal reported the 20 biggest buyback spenders in the first quarter are up over 5%, on average, since the start of the year to easily beat the S&P.
Richter points out there's an added tailwind to the buybacks, considering companies are bringing back cash from abroad under the Trump administration's new tax regime. While the idea was for companies to invest that money in growing their U.S. operations, it's not exactly playing out that way.
"Everyone knew this was a pretext for a corporate tax cut that would free companies to do what they'd done during the last 'repatriation holiday' in 2004: Buy back their own shares, increase dividends, and jack up executive compensation packages," Richter said, adding that the cash is a one-time treasure trove with limits to its benefits. "Once it's used up, it's gone. Then what?" he asked.
Richter, however, believes a crash will be avoided -- the good news -- but the stock market will instead "zig-zag" lower until the excesses have been wrung out, and that could take years -- the bad news.
For now, the Dow's streak is poised to continue...
The market
The Dow , S&P and Nasdaq are all up nicely in the early going. Gold is holding mostly steady while crude is leaning lower. Europe (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/european-stocks-slip-as-traders-watch-italian-politics-2018-05-14) is slipping as traders keep an eye news surrounding the new Italian government. Asia markets closed Monday's session mostly higher. Malaysian stocks were volatile () in the first session after a shocking election win for the opposition party.
See the latest in Market Snapshot (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/dow-futures-up-nearly-100-points-as-trump-helps-ease-trade-war-fears-2018-05-14)
The buzz
We're in the thick of commencement season, and some big names -- including Apple's Tim Cook (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ofhbdY7Ln1g) at Duke and Oprah Winfrey at USC -- have already dropped knowledge on college graduates across the country. There are plenty more notables on tap in the coming weeks, as well, such as Canadian PM Justin Trudeau at NYU and Facebook's (FB) Sheryl Sandberg at MIT, for instance.
Another senior Tesla (TSLA) executive has hit the road (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/teslas-safety-head-leaves-for-alphabets-self-driving-car-unit-waymo-2018-05-13). This time, it's Matthew Schwall, who was the company's main technical contact with U.S. safety regulators. He reportedly left Elon Musk and co. for rival Waymo LLC.
Xerox (XRX) is taking a hard hit after backing out of its merger deal (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/xerox-drops-fujifilm-merger-strikes-deal-with-activists-that-ousts-ceo-2018-05-13) with Fujifilm Holdings (4901.TO) as the iconic America company said it reached a new settlement with two of its biggest shareholders. Xerox said it would replace its chief executive and overhaul its board.
The chart
Tech industry analyst Horace Dediu tweeted out this chart (https://twitter.com/asymco/status/994132313939283968) of the fastest-growing tech platforms ever, including everything from iCould and Android to Netscape and China's bike-sharing program. Interestingly, it looks like that last one is eclipsing the first one in terms of pace of growth. The chart, broken down by quarter, shows how many users in millions a product had in the years after its launch.
The Quote:
"The greatest threat to American democracy isn't communism, jihadism, or any other external force or foreign power. It's our own willingness to tolerate dishonesty in service of party, and in pursuit of power" -- Michael Bloomberg talking to Rice University students (https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/wireStory/bloomberg-warns-epidemic-dishonesty-55117788) about what he calls the "epidemic of dishonesty."
The stat
21% -- That's how much marijuana jobs are expected to grow per year through 2022, according to the "2018 Marijuana Business Factbook (https://mjbizdaily.com/factbook/)." As it stands right now, about 125,000 to 160,000 people are employed by the cannabis industry, with that number expected to swell to 340,000 weed workers by 2022. To put that in perspective, health care is only expected to see jobs growth of about 2% per year over that period.
The economy
A quiet day is on tap in terms of data, with nothing on the slate of note. Retail sales hits on Tuesday, while housing starts and industrial production will be posted on Wednesday, highlighting a relatively sparse calendar all week. On Thursday, the New York Fed releases its first-quarter household debt and credit report.
Read: Inflation pause lends helping hand to borrowers (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/inflation-pause-lends-helping-hand-to-borrowers-2018-05-12).
Random reads
Top economic minds come together to deliver this list (https://www.thereadinglists.com/the-most-important-economics-books/) of the best books, including "Moneyball," on the topic ever written.
This is how a newspaper dies (https://www.politico.com/magazine/story/2018/05/13/denver-post-profits-newspaper-industry-218360).
"Melania" made some big strides among the most popular baby names (https://www.cnbc.com/2018/05/13/baby-name-melania-surged-in-popularity-in-2017--donald-unchanged.html) in 2017. "Donald," well, not so much.
Really, how hard could it be to repopulate the planet (https://www.wired.com/2018/05/geeks-guide-repopulate-planet/)?
Bill Gross's wife took a real Picasso off the couples wall and replaced it with a forgery (https://nypost.com/2018/05/11/wife-hung-fake-picasso-after-taking-real-thing-amid-contentious-divorce/) during contentious divorce.
A great stretch of holes by Tiger Woods over the weekend is giving his fans some hope that another major could happen (https://www.sbnation.com/golf/2018/5/13/17350116/tiger-woods-scores-players-championship-2018-results-tpc-sawgrass).
